section_summary: This section contains U.S. Office of War Information copies of Dōmei press digests dated September 13–20, 1943, followed by a December 31 consular despatch forwarding Japanese news bulletins distributed in Turkey and the enclosed bulletins dated December 1–8. The material combines Axis propaganda about economic development and political mobilization in Japanese-occupied Asia with exaggerated communiqués concerning China, Burma, New Guinea, the Gilbert and Solomon Islands, and Allied shipping losses. Recurring subjects include Philippine reconstruction, Indonesian volunteer forces, resource development, Subhas Chandra Bose and Indian independence, and Japanese claims of naval and aerial victories.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Press Service for the Pacific Zone, September 13, 1943 (continuation)
subfiles.from: Dōmei Press Service; distributed by the U.S. Office of War Information, New Delhi
subfiles.to: Information recipients in the Pacific Zone
subfiles.about: Reports concern financial controls in occupied China and economic development under Japanese rule in Sulawesi.
subfiles.summary: The continuation announces plans to reopen the China Securities Exchange and extend government purchasing and price controls to key commodities. A long item portrays the Japanese naval administration in Sulawesi as improving cotton production, local manufacturing, distribution, taxation, banking, and savings while keeping prices at prewar levels.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Press Service for the Pacific Zone, September 14, 1943
subfiles.from: Dōmei Press Service; distributed by the U.S. Office of War Information, New Delhi
subfiles.to: Information recipients in the Pacific Zone
subfiles.about: Reports describe administrative reorganization and volunteer-defense agitation in Indonesia and industrial growth in Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin announces new traffic and communications boards in Sumatra and publicizes petitions and newspaper support for Muslim and Indonesian volunteer defense corps in Java. It also presents Minoru Aoki's account of large wartime increases in Manchukuo's steel, coal, copper, and zinc production and of extensive Japanese investment in heavy industry.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Press Service for the Pacific Zone, September 15, 1943
subfiles.from: Dōmei Press Service; distributed by the U.S. Office of War Information, New Delhi
subfiles.to: Information recipients in the Pacific Zone
subfiles.about: Items address a Borneo pulp industry, Japanese–French Indochinese mail, Chinese price measures, and enemy property claims in the Philippines.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin says paper mills will be established at Tawau and other Borneo ports after forests were judged suitable for pulp. It reports a provisional postal agreement between Japan and French Indochina, Ambassador Masayuki Tani's praise of Chinese emergency economic controls, and a deadline for Filipinos to register claims against property seized as enemy-owned.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Press Service for the Pacific Zone, September 16, 1943
subfiles.from: Dōmei and Nanpō Dōmei press services; distributed by the U.S. Office of War Information, New Delhi
subfiles.to: Information recipients in the Pacific Zone
subfiles.about: Reports cover Philippine transportation, Italian residents in China, reconstruction projects, Japanese films in Malaya, and a planned Tawau paper mill.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin celebrates the reconstruction of Philippine railways, roads, bridges, and a Mindoro pier under Japanese occupation. It inventories Italian residents, diplomatic offices, investments, and concessions in China following Italy's surrender. Shorter reports promote Japanese war films in Singapore and repeat plans for paper manufacturing in North Borneo.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Press Service for the Pacific Zone, September 17, 1943
subfiles.from: Dōmei and Nanpō Dōmei press services; distributed by the U.S. Office of War Information, New Delhi
subfiles.to: Information recipients in the Pacific Zone
subfiles.about: A broad economic digest reports Philippine banking and production, Manchukuo industry, Chinese railways, Thai youth policy, and Malayan resource development.
subfiles.summary: Philippine items describe new rural bank agencies, schools, copper and agricultural projects, and government-owned corporations. Reports from Manchukuo concern a small blast furnace, new economic advisers, and increased wool production, while other items cover a continental railway conference and Thailand's proposed national youth movement. Malayan and Bornean stories promote limestone products, a local medicinal plant, and revived insurance business.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Press Service for the Pacific Zone, September 18, 1943
subfiles.from: Dōmei and Nanpō Dōmei press services; distributed by the U.S. Office of War Information, New Delhi
subfiles.to: Information recipients in the Pacific Zone
subfiles.about: The bulletin emphasizes Philippine reconstruction and agriculture, Chinese economic regulation, a Javanese visit to Japan, and administrative measures in Southeast Asia.
subfiles.summary: Several articles portray Mindanao reconstruction, rising Philippine revenue, expanded cotton growing, shipping, forestry, schools, and employment for former soldiers as evidence of successful occupation. Chinese reports announce severe anti-profiteering penalties and a plan to drain part of Lake Taihu for farming. Other items follow a Java inspection party in Japan, village sports grounds near Solo, Malayan currency exchange rules, and plans for fish canneries at Pangkor Island.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Press Service for the Pacific Zone, September 19, 1943
subfiles.from: Dōmei Press Service; distributed by the U.S. Office of War Information, New Delhi
subfiles.to: Information recipients in the Pacific Zone
subfiles.about: Brief items concern wooden shipbuilding in Manchukuo, Japanese produce supplies, and wrestlers performing dock labor.
subfiles.summary: The Manchukuo Labour Association proposes training a 300-man carpenters' corps for work at southern shipyards. Japanese food reports compare potato, radish, citrus, lettuce, and apple harvests, while a labor item praises professional wrestlers unloading rice at Tokyo Harbour.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Press Service for the Pacific Zone, September 20, 1943
subfiles.from: Dōmei Press Service; distributed by the U.S. Office of War Information, New Delhi
subfiles.to: Information recipients in the Pacific Zone
subfiles.about: Reports praise rural conditions and economic reconstruction in the Philippines and promote Muslim military cooperation and remittance controls in the Netherlands East Indies.
subfiles.summary: Benito M. Sakdalan claims that Filipino farmers receive better prices and improved relations with landlords under the occupation, while another item describes industrial and agricultural expansion in the Visayas. Hadji Hammul urges Java's Muslims to join a volunteer defense corps alongside Japan and is profiled as a widely respected religious teacher. A final item announces expanded rules for remittances between Java, the Southern Regions, China, Manchukuo, and the Kwantung territory.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2140 (R-1988): Transmitting Some Japanese News Bulletins Distributed in Turkey
subfiles.from: Roy M. Melbourne, American Vice Consul, Istanbul
subfiles.about: The vice consul forwards Japanese daily news bulletins issued in Turkey during December 1943.
subfiles.summary: Melbourne encloses Japanese bulletins that he believes may contain useful information beyond the regular military communiqués. The despatch identifies the enclosures and notes distribution of the original and hectograph copies within the State Department.

subfiles.title: Bulletin d'informations, Agence Dōmei, December 1, 1943
subfiles.about: The French-language bulletin alleges Allied attacks on Japanese hospital ships and claims major naval victories near the Gilbert Islands.
subfiles.summary: Japan's Information Board protests through Spain and Switzerland against alleged Anglo-American attacks on hospital ships, listing individual ships, locations, and damage. A second item gives inflated Japanese claims for Allied aircraft carriers, cruisers, destroyers, transports, and aircraft destroyed or damaged in the Gilbert Islands fighting, while acknowledging twenty-seven Japanese aircraft lost.

subfiles.title: The Dōmei News, December 1, 1943
subfiles.about: The English-language bulletin recounts the alleged fourth air battle off the Gilberts and announces senior Japanese naval appointments.
subfiles.summary: A naval correspondent gives a dramatic account of torpedo attacks on an American task force and repeats claims that twenty-two ships and 125 aircraft were destroyed or damaged in nine days. The bulletin then announces the reassignment of Admirals Nobutake Kondo and Zengo Yoshida and Vice Admirals Denshichi Okawachi, Masaichi Niimi, Sakae Tokunaga, and Yukitake Nikaido. Biographical sketches emphasize their earlier commands in China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Bulletin d'informations, Agence Dōmei, December 2, 1943
subfiles.about: Military communiqués claim Japanese advances at Changde and victories in Burma, eastern India, and New Guinea.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin says Japanese forces are encircling Chinese reinforcements near Changde and predicts the stronghold's imminent fall. It also lists enemy casualties and captured ammunition in the Hukawng area, claims eight Allied aircraft destroyed at Akoba, and reports three B-24 bombers shot down near Alexishafen.

subfiles.title: The Dōmei News, December 2, 1943
subfiles.about: Items cover a Singapore industrial exhibition, Pacific air raids, citations for Japanese units in Hubei, and Indian independence propaganda.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin promotes a Chinese industrial exposition in Singapore and claims damage to Allied shipping and installations near Mono and Bougainville. It recounts Japanese ground operations in Hubei and Hunan to justify imperial citations for Sasamoto Company and Tobita's squad. Further reports say Subhas Chandra Bose thanked Ramon de Valera for famine assistance and describe Manila celebrations of Japan's promised transfer of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands to the Provisional Government of Free India.

subfiles.title: Bulletin d'informations, Agence Dōmei, December 3, 1943
subfiles.about: The bulletin presents Bose's plans to move his government toward Burma and outlines educational decrees in the occupied Philippines.
subfiles.summary: Subhas Chandra Bose tells a Singapore rally that the Provisional Government of Free India will soon move to Burma as the Indian National Army advances toward the frontier. He praises the Greater East Asia declaration, Japan's promised transfer of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and preparations for a final independence struggle. A second item summarizes Philippine decrees on teacher qualifications, Tagalog instruction, and stronger government control of private and foreign-run schools.

subfiles.title: The Dōmei News, December 3, 1943
subfiles.about: The bulletin reports Indian National Army recruitment and publishes Kurusu's attack on the U.S. account of the 1941 Japanese-American negotiations.
subfiles.summary: A short Kuching item describes a send-off for volunteers joining Bose's Indian National Army. The remainder quotes Saburō Kurusu at length, alleging that the American white paper suppressed Roosevelt's proposal to act as an introducer between Japan and China and misrepresented Japan's November 1941 offer. Kurusu portrays Cordell Hull and the U.S. government as evasive and deceptive and asserts confidence in Japan's Greater East Asia program.

subfiles.title: The Dōmei News, December 4, 1943
subfiles.about: Reports announce political participation under the naval administration and explain the strategic and economic importance of captured Changde and the Hunan–Hubei region.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin previews regulations allowing limited native political participation in territories under Japanese naval administration. It celebrates the fall of Changde, describing its routes, Chinese defenses, agricultural production, and value as a supply base. A broader analysis depicts Hunan and Hubei as China's rice bowl and emphasizes the region's antimony, iron, manganese, and tungsten resources.

subfiles.title: Bulletin d'informations, Agence Dōmei, evening edition, December 6, 1943
subfiles.about: The bulletin claims a major carrier victory off Bougainville and reports statements by a captured Chinese correspondent and anti-guerrilla operations in Shandong.
subfiles.summary: A commentary on the alleged sixth air battle off Bougainville claims the United States lost additional carriers and that its southwest Pacific fleet had been paralyzed. Captured correspondent Teng Shou-hsin is quoted as saying Chongqing's youth increasingly recognized the futility of resistance and that poorly trained Chinese troops lacked fighting spirit. A final communiqué lists casualties, prisoners, and captured weapons in operations by a collaborationist Chinese peace-preservation unit in western Shandong.

subfiles.title: The Dōmei News, December 6, 1943
subfiles.about: Items cover a Java press levy, Japanese naval claims, anniversary celebrations in Malaya, anti-Communist operations in China, and an air raid on Kolkata.
subfiles.summary: Java newspapers agree to add ten sen to subscriptions for the island's air-defense army, while Tokyo sources claim twenty-six Allied vessels and 145 aircraft destroyed or damaged around the Gilbert and Marshall Islands. Kuala Lumpur and Malacca prepare multiethnic events marking the war's second anniversary. Further reports claim joint Japanese and collaborationist successes in Hubei and heavy damage to ships and port facilities during an army-navy air raid on Kolkata.

subfiles.title: Bulletin d'informations, Agence Dōmei, December 6, 1943
subfiles.about: Two imperial headquarters communiqués claim Allied aircraft losses across Asia and announce Changde's capture.
subfiles.summary: The first communiqué aggregates alleged Allied aircraft losses in Burma, New Guinea, and China between November 25 and December 2. The second announces Changde's capitulation and lists Chinese troops, aircraft, artillery, machine guns, and rifles allegedly destroyed or captured during the campaign, alongside 556 Japanese dead.

subfiles.title: Bulletin d'informations, Agence Dōmei, December 8, 1943, evening material of December 7
subfiles.about: The bulletin gives cumulative Japanese naval victory claims, announces Thai constitution celebrations, and reports Gotaro Ogawa's proposed advisory post in Burma.
subfiles.summary: Dōmei statistics claim 688 Allied warships and hundreds of other vessels sunk or damaged since the war began, along with 6,874 aircraft destroyed, and provide detailed breakdowns of enemy and Japanese losses. A Bangkok item describes three days of constitution-anniversary events, including a renamed beauty contest. Tokyo reports that financier and politician Gotaro Ogawa will be recommended as supreme adviser to the Burmese government.

subfiles.title: The Dōmei News, December 7, 1943
subfiles.about: The surviving page reports Japanese diplomatic travel, aerial combat over Changde, an imperial commendation for the Combined Fleet, and appointments to Singapore's advisory board.
subfiles.summary: Shigenori Tashiro leaves Saigon for consultations with Ambassador Kenkichi Yoshizawa in Hanoi. A military report claims Japanese fighters shot down or damaged American aircraft over Changde, and another says the emperor commended the Combined Fleet's air arm for operations near the Gilbert Islands. The page ends during an item naming Chinese, Malay, Indian, Eurasian, and other members of Singapore's first consultative board.
